brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to CTFS - For TechIQ Attendees

questions.question: How many major buyer personas will you encounter at TechIQ?
choices: Two personas: clinical operations and IT leadership
Three personas: Gilbert, Reena, and Andres
Four personas: Gilbert, Reena, Andres, and one additional stakeholder
Five personas representing all major sponsor departments
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—Gilbert, Reena, and Andres are the three primary personas you'll meet, each with distinct financial pain points.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course identifies three primary personas at TechIQ. While there are four personas mentioned in the materials overall, the focus at the event is on Gilbert (Clinical Operations), Reena (VP IT Clinical), and Andres (Digital Transformation).

questions.question: What is the primary problem that CTFS Contracting solves in the clinical trial workflow?
choices: It automates site recruitment and enrollment processes
It reduces manual contract execution delays and eliminates duplicate data entry between systems
It manages investigator budgets using 38 million negotiated data points
It forecasts real-time trial costs using historical spend data
questions.feedback_correct: You've identified the core problem correctly—Contracting streamlines the manual, error-prone CTA process and connects contract terms directly to payment systems.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While CTFS has multiple modules, Contracting specifically solves the contract execution bottleneck. GrantPlan handles budgeting, and Forecasting handles cost projection—but Contracting eliminates the manual handoffs between contract signing and payment processing.

questions.question: What are the three versions of the CTFS pitch you should prepare, and what distinguishes them?
choices: Short, medium, and long versions differentiated by the number of modules you mention
Versions for clinical ops, IT, and digital transformation stakeholders
Under 35 words for hallway conversations, under 75 words for five-minute chats, under 150 words for formal meetings
Versions with and without competitive comparisons, plus one for skeptical buyers
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—the pitch discipline is about fitting the moment, not the audience. Word count and context dictate which version you deliver.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The three pitch versions are structured by context and time available, not by persona or content focus. Each version leads with the customer's problem before naming the solution, but the depth increases with the time you have available.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a discovery question designed to open a real conversation with a buyer persona?
choices: For Gilbert: How are payment delays affecting your site relationships right now?
For Reena: What keeps you up at night from a compliance risk standpoint?
For Andres: Can you tell me about your current technology stack and budget for new platforms?
For Andres: Where are your current AI investments stalling before they reach scale?
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—asking directly about technology stack and budget is transactional, not discovery. The best discovery questions focus on the buyer's specific pain and priorities in their own language.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes discovery questions that are open, specific to the person's world, and focused on their pain—not on your solution or their procurement process. Questions about pain, frustration, and roadblocks open doors; questions about budgets and systems close them down.

questions.question: Why does the course emphasize that Contracting is 'not a standalone tool'?
choices: Because it requires integration with at least two other CTFS modules to function
Because signed CTAs automatically inform payment milestones in Site Payments and update budget alignment in GrantPlan without manual re-entry
Because it depends on manual reconciliation between contract terms and payment schedules
Because sponsors typically use multiple contract management tools alongside CTFS
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the power of Contracting lies in its integration. A signed contract automatically triggers downstream actions, eliminating the duplicate data entry that point solutions require.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The 'not standalone' distinction is crucial because it highlights CTFS's competitive advantage over point solutions. Contracting connects directly to the downstream financial systems, creating an end-to-end unified flow rather than isolated tools that require manual handoffs.

questions.question: What is the core value proposition that separates CTFS from competing point solutions?
choices: CTFS has the largest database of negotiated investigator rates in the market
CTFS solves the entire financial lifecycle and eliminates the data handoff friction that point solutions require
CTFS uses more advanced AI algorithms than competing platforms
CTFS supports more geographies than any other clinical trial finance vendor
questions.feedback_correct: That's the unification story—point solutions solve one problem well but create integration problems on either side. CTFS covers the whole lifecycle without the friction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While CTFS has many strengths individually, the course emphasizes that its competitive win is the unification story. Point solutions force you to reconcile between systems; CTFS eliminates that burden by connecting budgeting, contracting, payments, and forecasting in one platform.

questions.question: If a buyer says 'We already have a system,' what is the recommended approach to move the conversation forward?
choices: Acknowledge that you understand and offer to compare CTFS features against their existing system
Ask what their current system does NOT unify, then quantify the cost of that gap
Pivot immediately to discussing the Contracting module as a complementary tool
Suggest a sandbox pilot to demonstrate CTFS's capabilities directly
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—the gap question is the key. It opens a real conversation because the honest answer almost always reveals unification problems that cost money.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course teaches you to avoid feature comparison and instead dig into the gaps that existing systems create. By asking what doesn't unify, you redirect the conversation from 'we have something already' to 'here's what we're still struggling with,' which is where CTFS wins.

questions.question: What constitutes a qualified TechIQ lead according to the course?
choices: Any buyer who shows interest in hearing a CTFS demonstration
A buyer who expresses pain around financial processes AND you've identified a named decision-maker willing to continue the conversation, OR they show openness to a pilot within 30 days
A buyer who commits to a follow-up meeting before leaving the booth
A buyer from the top 20 pharma companies who use IQVIA for other services
questions.feedback_correct: Precisely—qualification requires both expressed pain AND a real mechanism to continue (named decision-maker, openness to demo, budget visibility, or pilot interest). One strong signal is enough.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not every good conversation is a qualified opportunity. The course emphasizes specific markers: expressed pain, a named decision-maker or influencer willing to continue, openness to a demo/pilot within 30 days, or budget authority/visibility. These signals tell you whether to invest follow-up effort.

questions.question: What should you do immediately after a meaningful TechIQ conversation to preserve critical information?
choices: Send a follow-up email to the contact within 24 hours summarizing what you discussed
Enter the conversation into your CRM system at the end of the day with all relevant details
Take a 90-second voice memo or note the persona, stated pain, qualifying signals, and agreed next step right after the conversation
Request a calendar invitation for the next meeting before either of you leave the conversation
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—capture insights immediately while they're fresh, not at the end of the day when details blur together. A quick voice memo preserves the specificity that makes follow-up personalized and effective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course stresses urgency: capture information right after the conversation, not hours later. By the end of TechIQ, you'll have had eight more conversations and the specific details will be lost. A quick memo captures the persona, their exact pain in their words, qualifying signals, and the next step you agreed on.

questions.question: How should a 30-day follow-up plan be structured, and what makes it effective?
choices: A generic email to all TechIQ contacts offering a product demonstration and inviting them to schedule a call

Contact name and title, personalized follow-up action referencing their specific pain, and a target date within 30 days with a clear milestone (scheduled call, CRM opportunity, or pilot invitation accepted)
A series of automated nurture emails sent to all qualified leads with rotating content about CTFS modules
Monthly check-ins with all TechIQ contacts to maintain relationship engagement until budget cycles align
questions.feedback_correct: You've got it—the follow-up plan combines personalization (referencing their exact pain) with structure (clear action and date) and measurable outcomes (specific milestone targets). Generic follow-up goes nowhere.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes that follow-up must be personalized, not generic. Each contact needs a specific action tied to their stated pain, a target date, and a milestone that proves progress. This structure converts good conversations into actual pipeline opportunities instead of interesting memories.
